Yesterday we decoupled storage from compute and settled the ETL-vs-ELT question.
Both of those still assumed a comfortable premise: data arrives, sits somewhere,
and gets processed **later**. Today we break that premise.

Most of the data an AI system actually cares about — a user's click, a sensor
reading, a credit-card swipe, a chat message arriving mid-conversation — is not
useful "later." A fraud model that flags a stolen card six hours after the
purchase has already failed. A recommendation engine that updates your feed
once a day feels broken compared to one that adapts on your very next scroll.
**Real-time data engineering is the discipline of treating data as a
continuous, never-ending flow of individual events, and processing each one
within milliseconds of it happening — not storing it to process in bulk
tonight.**

This matters even more once AI is in the loop. LLM inference is slow relative
to a database query — a call can take seconds, not milliseconds — and
multi-agent systems chain many of those calls together. A traditional
synchronous request-response design blocks a whole thread on every one of
them. Event-driven, streaming architectures are how production AI systems
absorb that latency without falling over: producers publish events and move
on, brokers hold the backlog safely, and consumers — including AI models —
process at their own pace, scaling up or down independently.
